European shag chicks emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] after an average interval of 30.5 days [ab = 30.5 days]. This developmental period aligns closely with incubation durations documented among congeners nesting in temperate North Atlantic colonies. Upon hatching, these altricial nestlings weigh approximately 35.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 35.8 grams], a modest neonatal mass that underscores the species' reliance on sustained biparental provisioning during the early weeks of post-hatching growth. The newly emerged chicks are brooded intensively, and their initial mass represents only a small fraction of the adult body size they will eventually attain.

As the nestling period progresses, the young birds undergo a phase of rapid mass increase, ultimately reaching a maximum adult body mass of 1990 grams [Wwi = 1990 grams]. This substantial gain in mass is fueled by the frequent delivery of lipid-rich fish prey by both parents, a strategy common among pursuit-diving seabirds. The transition from a hatchling mass of just over 35 grams to an asymptote approaching two kilograms reflects the high energetic demands of developing flight musculature and insulating plumage necessary for independent foraging in cold coastal waters. Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species (40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]), fledging occurs at 47 days after hatching [tx = 47 days after hatching], marking the point at which the young bird achieves its first flight. This milestone is preceded by the completion of feather development and a period of wing-exercise behaviour around the nest site.

Sexual maturation in European shag follows a more protracted timeline compared to the rapid somatic development of the nestling phase. At a body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], puberty is estimated to occur at 141 days after hatching [tp = 141 days after hatching], a stage coinciding with the completion of skeletal growth and the onset of gonadal activity in immature individuals. Despite reaching physiological reproductive capacity relatively early in their second half-year, most young shags do not immediately engage in breeding. Instead, they typically delay their first successful nesting attempt until 730 days after hatching [tR = 730 days after hatching] at 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], a delay that is commonly attributed to the time required to acquire sufficient foraging proficiency and to secure a breeding territory within a crowded colony.

Reproductive output in this species is modest by avian standards, reflecting a life-history strategy oriented toward high offspring survival rather than fecundity. Females lay 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 eggs per clutch] and typically produce 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = 1 clutch per year], a relatively low annual reproductive rate that is consistent with the species' extended period of parental care and its dependence on seasonally abundant prey stocks. This annual output, achieved under the metabolic conditions associated with a body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], results in a limited number of offspring per breeding season. The combination of a fixed clutch size and a single annual reproductive event places strong selective pressure on the survival of each nestling, favouring robust parental investment in provisioning and predator defence.

Longevity records for the European shag indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 30.6 years [am = approximately 30.6 years] when measured under free-ranging conditions at a typical active body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This extended lifespan, remarkable for a bird of its size, is characteristic of many long-lived seabirds that exhibit low adult mortality rates and delayed senescence. The combination of a late age at first reproduction, modest annual fecundity, and exceptional longevity places the shag firmly within the slow end of the life-history continuum, a pattern shaped by the ecological constraints of marine foraging in a variable environment. Comparative analyses with other Phalacrocorax species suggest that this lifespan is near the upper bound for the genus, reflecting adaptations to a relatively predation-free adult existence and a reliable food supply.
